raw_case_text: We report a case of a 56-year-old man presenting acute fever, cutaneous rash, conjunctival hyperemia, intense joint pain, and self-reported use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) in the initial days of symptoms. The patient reported that for the last 30 days before Hospital admission, he started presenting fever, headaches, paresthesia, and pain in the right arm with visible red spots on the skin. These skin lesions worsened and spread through the lower limbs and trunk within a period of 10 days. The patient evolved to hypotension with some Hospital admissions and discharges. On the 15th day after skin disease onset, he developed thrombocytopenia, liver dysfunction with International Normalized Ratio (INR) of 1.45 and Prothrombin Time of 56%, edema in his hands and feet and hemorrhagic bullous lesions on the skin of the upper and lower limbs (Figures 1a-c), being admitted to the Intensive Care Unit. Immediately, therapy was started with meropenem and vancomycin, then maintained for 6 days, during which the patient presented some febrile peaks. Subsequently, intravenous administration of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (Human), 5% (Flebogamma  5% DIF, Instituto Grifols S.A., Barcelona, Spain) at 400 mg/Kg/day restarted for 5 days. Antibiotic therapy started again for 5 days. The patient showed a progressive increase in platelet levels from 43,000 to 201,000 and total leukocyte count, together with an important reductions of the edema, necrosis, and erythema. Ten days after globulin administration, a substantial improvement of the bullous lesions was observed (Figures 1g-l). The patient evolved with aphasia, thus being considered to be suffering a transient acute ischemic stroke. Laboratory analysis followed the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) recommendations, in which a single anti-CHIKV IgM-positive test (collected during acute or convalescence phase) is sufficient for confirmation of any suspected case of CHIKV. The blood test returned positive serology for Dengue (IgM-/IgG+) and Chikungunya (IgM+) at the 16th day after symptom onset, but results were negative for other infectious diseases and blood culture. Notably, laboratory tests excluded other confounding diseases such as: malaria, leptospirosis, rheumatic fever, septic arthritis, Zika, and Mayaro. Moreover, there is no report showing any Mayaro case detected in the state of Paraiba. This would definitively exclude the possibility of a cross-reactive IgM serology against another alphavirus as discussed elsewhere. No comorbidities were reported, except for alcoholism. Throughout hospitalization, imaging exams were normal and no vasoactive drugs were administered. Furthermore, no lesions were observed in oral, genital, or conjunctival mucosa. Nikolsky's sign was positive. A diagnosis of Stevens Johnson syndrome-Toxic epidermal necrolysis-like features was discarded. The patient was discharged and has not presented any other clinical sign of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old man presented with a 30-day history of fever, headache, intense arthralgia, conjunctival hyperemia, and progressive generalized erythematous skin lesions that evolved into limb edema and hemorrhagic bullae.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Thirty days prior to ICU admission, the patient developed acute fever, headache, paresthesia, intense joint pain, conjunctival hyperemia, and red skin spots on the right arm, and self-medicated with NSAIDs during the initial days. Over 10 days, the skin lesions worsened and spread across his lower limbs and trunk, accompanied by episodes of hypotension across multiple brief hospital admissions. On day 15 of skin disease onset, he developed thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy/liver dysfunction, hand and foot edema, and extensive hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions on the upper and lower extremities, prompting ICU admission. During hospitalization, he also experienced transient aphasia attributed to a transient acute ischemic stroke.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of alcoholism; no other medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, paresthesia, right arm pain, intense arthralgia, conjunctival hyperemia, progressive bullous skin rash, hand/foot edema, and transient aphasia; negative for oral, genital, or conjunctival mucosal ulceration. Prior medication: self-administered NSAIDs at symptom onset.

objective.physical_examination: Hypotension prior to ICU admission; conjunctival hyperemia; marked edema of the hands and feet; extensive erythematous, necrotic, and hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions over the upper and lower limbs with a positive Nikolsky's sign. Oral, genital, and conjunctival mucosae were spared (no mucosal lesions). Transient aphasia observed during hospitalization.
objective.routine_investigations: Coagulation/hepatic tests (day 15): INR 1.45, prothrombin time (PT) 56%, and liver dysfunction. Complete blood count: thrombocytopenia (nadir 43,000/mm3, later rising to 201,000/mm3). Blood cultures: negative. Infectious and rheumatologic screening for malaria, leptospirosis, rheumatic fever, septic arthritis, Zika, and Mayaro viruses: negative. Imaging studies during hospitalization: normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe atypical acute chikungunya infection presenting with extensive vesiculobullous/hemorrhagic cutaneous eruption (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis-like bullous dermatosis without mucosal involvement) and transient ischemic stroke. Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN was ruled out due to complete mucosal sparing, and active dengue, Zika, Mayaro, malaria, leptospirosis, septic arthritis, and bacterial sepsis were excluded. Confirmation: Positive serum anti-CHIKV IgM and past dengue exposure (Dengue IgM-negative / IgG-positive) on day 16 of illness per PAHO criteria. Management and outcome: Treated in the ICU with empiric IV meropenem and vancomycin (for 6 days, plus a subsequent 5-day antibiotic course) and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 5%, 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days) without requiring vasopressors. Platelet counts recovered from 43,000 to 201,000/mm3, limb edema and hemorrhagic bullae markedly regressed within 10 days of IVIG, and the patient was discharged completely recovered with no residual sequelae.
